1-2: A square of two by two cells drawn with all its lines: the small squares and the big one around them.
A figure of cells shaped like a cross or a letter: the squares of one cell and the bigger squares made of several.
A square with both its diagonals drawn: the small triangles and those made of two pieces.
A square with one diagonal and one line through its middle: the triangles in it, small and large.
A triangle with one line from a corner to the opposite side: the two pieces and the whole triangle.
A triangle with two or three lines from its top corner down to its base: the triangles of one, two or more pieces.
A big triangle with one line across it from side to side: the triangles in the drawing, the whole one too.
A house drawn as a square under a triangle roof, with a line down its middle: the triangles in the drawing.
Matches laid along the sides of a row of squares, a shared side one match: how many matches the picture holds.
Matches laid as squares, some of them drawn dashed: the squares still whole when the dashed matches are taken away.
Matches laid as a row of squares: the fewest matches to take away so that no square is left whole.
3-4: A square of cells with some of its cells cut out: the squares of every size whose cells are all still there.
A square of cells with one cell marked: the squares of every size that hold the marked cell.
A square of cells with one diagonal drawn across the whole of it: the squares of every size the diagonal does not cut.
A right triangle drawn on squared paper with the paper's lines inside it: the whole squares that lie inside it.
Several squares drawn overlapping on squared paper: the squares whose four sides all lie on the drawn lines.
A triangle with lines from its top corner to its base and one or two lines across it: the triangles of every size.
A rectangle with both its diagonals and the two lines through its middle: the triangles of every size.
A square of two by two cells with a diagonal drawn in each cell: the triangles of every size.
Matches laid along every side of the cells of a figure, some taken away: the squares of every size still whole.
Matches laid as a few squares in a figure: the matches that are a side of two squares at once.
Matches laid as a square of two by two cells: the fewest to take away so that only the big outer square is left whole.
5-6: A rectangle of cells drawn with all its lines: the squares of every size, counted size by size.
Points drawn at some corners of squared paper: the squares, tilted ones too, whose four corners are all drawn points.
A figure of lines on squared paper: the triangles and the squares whose sides lie on the lines, and which there are more of.
A square with the square joining the middles of its sides drawn inside it, and its diagonals: the triangles of every size.
A figure of triangles drawn on squared paper with one cell marked: the triangles that hold the marked cell.
A square cut into triangles by lines that meet only at corners of the paper: the triangles made of exactly two pieces.
Squares and lines drawn on squared paper, some cells shaded: the largest square on the drawn lines that holds no shaded cell.
Matches laid as a square of three by three cells: the fewest to take away so that no square of any size is left whole.
Matches laid as a figure of squares: the fewest matches to move so that every square is the same size and no match is loose.
Matches laid as a figure of squares: the fewest to take away so that the squares left share no match.
Matches laid on squared paper: the fewest matches to add so that every match is a side of a whole square.
